platforms.title: Sudden Facial Drooping Isn't Always What You Think
platforms.meta_description: Waking up with one side of your face not moving could be Bell's palsy or a stroke. How checking your forehead tells the two apart.
platforms.body_html:
Ever woken up with one side of your face drooping and your eye not closing all the way? It's easy to panic and not know whether to rush to the ER or wait it out, but Mayo Clinic points to a simple first check: can you wrinkle your forehead? Bell's palsy and stroke both start with facial drooping on one side, but they're very different emergencies underneath.

Why the forehead is the key difference

Forehead muscles receive nerve signals from both sides of the brain. So with a stroke, where the problem sits inside the brain, the opposite side of the brain keeps controlling the forehead, which means the lower face droops while the forehead still wrinkles normally and the eyebrow still lifts. Bell's palsy, on the other hand, comes from inflammation of the facial nerve itself (cranial nerve VII), not the brain, so the entire side of the face droops from forehead to mouth. Whether you can wrinkle your forehead is the fastest self-check that tells the two apart.

Bell's palsy tends to show up after a cold or upper respiratory infection, or more often in the later stages of pregnancy, and it's generally thought to involve nerve inflammation linked to reactivation of the herpes simplex virus. Symptoms typically appear suddenly within 48 hours, which is part of why it looks so alarming — that speed mimics a stroke on the surface.

What to actually do about it

First, if the forehead won't wrinkle and the whole side of the face droops, Bell's palsy is more likely — but if the forehead is spared while only the lower face droops, or if arm or leg weakness shows up too, treat it as a possible stroke and get to an emergency room immediately. Every minute spent hesitating can cost stroke treatment its window.

Second, if it turns out to be Bell's palsy, starting corticosteroids within 72 hours of symptom onset matters most. Mayo Clinic notes that treatment started within that window leads to noticeably better recovery outcomes.

Third, use artificial tears often on the side that won't close, and protect the eye at night with an eye patch or tape. An eye that can't fully close is at real risk of corneal drying and damage — a complication that's easy to overlook next to the more obvious facial weakness.

Most people with Bell's palsy recover fully within three to six months, even without any treatment at all, though a smaller number are left with some lingering weakness or occasional involuntary muscle movement on the affected side. Recurrence is uncommon but not impossible, so a second episode later in life doesn't necessarily mean anything more serious is going on. If both sides of the face droop at once, or if numbness spreads beyond the face, that points away from a typical Bell's palsy pattern and toward a different neurological cause that needs its own workup.

The bottom line: if one side of your face suddenly droops, look in a mirror and try to wrinkle your forehead first. A normal forehead points toward Bell's palsy, but still check for other stroke signs — arm or leg weakness, slurred speech — and go to the ER immediately if there's any doubt. This article is general health information; see a doctor for diagnosis and treatment.
